results.title: 7 Secrets to Growing "Infinite" Bell Peppers (No Digging!)
results.description:
What if you didn't have to pull up your bell pepper plants every fall and start over from seed?

Most gardeners treat bell peppers as annual plants, but they're actually tender perennials — meaning they can live and produce for multiple years when protected from freezing temperatures. With the right overwintering strategy, that same pepper plant can come back season after season with an established root system and a major head start.

In this video, you'll discover 7 secrets to keeping bell pepper plants productive for multiple seasons — without digging them up.

🌱 Understand the perennial nature of peppers and why frost, rather than the plant's natural lifespan, is the main limitation.

🪴 Grow peppers in containers so you can move the entire plant indoors before freezing weather arrives.

❄️ Bring peppers inside for winter and learn how allowing them to rest semi-dormant can make overwintering much easier.

☀️ Wake your pepper plant gradually in spring so it can transition safely back into active growth.

✂️ Prune young growth to encourage a bushier plant with more potential flowering and fruiting sites.

🫑 Harvest regularly to keep your pepper plant producing throughout the growing season.

🌿 Feed consistently so an established pepper plant has the nutrients it needs for extended growth and fruit production.

The goal isn't literally to grow an "infinite" pepper plant. It's to stop treating a naturally perennial plant like a disposable annual and give it the opportunity to live for several growing seasons.

Imagine reaching your third summer with the same established bell pepper plant, already equipped with a mature root system and woody structure instead of starting from seed all over again.

If you live somewhere with freezing winters, protecting the plant from frost is the key. If you garden in a warm climate where peppers can survive outdoors year-round, the process can be even simpler.

results.title: Don’t Throw Away Your Pepper Plants - Overwinter Them!
results.description:
Your pepper plants will survive until next year if you do THESE things! Peppers are actually perennial plants, but the problem is that most of the climates we have here in America don’t support their survival through the winter season. But if we could show you how to overwinter them correctly, you can save your plants until next year and have a BIG head start on next year’s abundant pepper harvest! You will first need to pick the rest of the peppers that are on the plant. Harvest them all, even the smallest ones. Then you’ll do some heavy pruning. There are bumps on the stems called nodes, and Dan will show you where exactly to prune your pepper plant based on the location of the nodes. After it’s pruned way down, you will place it in a pot, add some topsoil to the level of where the ground came to previously on the plant, and add some fertilizer and minerals. The important thing is to nourish the roots with what you add, while not adding anything that would encourage leaf growth. We’ll place our pruned pepper plants in a specific temperature range, and then in the spring we’ll teach you what to look for in the weather for the perfect time to replant them in your garden. And then next spring you’ll have all that growth as a head start toward a new year of pepper harvest!

Welcome to Joyful Homestead! We're Dan and Heidi, and it's our passion to live as independently as we can on our land, grow and preserve much of our own food, raise productive chickens, and make our own items from nature such as teas and salves that enhance our health. Our second passion is to teach people what we've learned in each of these categories! Come learn along with us!

results.title: Overwintering My Potted Plants 2026
results.description:
I'm bringing my potted Buena Mulata, Anaheim, and bay laurel indoors for winter 2026–2027. After a family-emergency break, this is the practical plan: which plants stay, which California Wonder can finish and go, pest checks so I don't infest the houseplants, and a warm west-window shelf instead of a near-freezing hibernation setup I don't have.

In this video I walk through:
* Why Buena Mulata and Anaheim are keepers (and why bay laurel is slow-growing enough to save)
* Why I'm skipping a full California Wonder overwinter (sweet bells are harder; seed-starting is easy)
* Timing around mid to low 50s °F nights in southeast Michigan, plus daily pest watching before move-in
* Windstorm trauma on the peppers while I was away
* Close-ups of Buena Mulata, Anaheim, and the recently potted-up bay laurel
* Indoor shelf setup: former hydro cilantro space, jade plants, west window, and a ~30 W two-foot grow light for keep-alive (not winter fruiting)

This is my observed active-overwinter plan in a ~70 °F house. I'm not doing cool garage dormancy here because an unheated garage drops below freezing. Treat pest inspect and quarantine seriously before anything sits next to houseplants.
